Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
Carol had always been the kind of person who noticed details—a useful trait in her work as a policy analyst for the state environmental agency. But the noticing changed after the incident at the chemical storage facility, the one she’d been sent to evaluate for a routine compliance review. The fire started small, a spark from a faulty ventilation motor near a row of solvent drums. She remembered the acrid sweetness that filled the air first—a smell like burnt alcohol and scorched plastic—before the alarms went off. By the time she reached the stairwell, the smoke was thick and chemical-laden, and she could taste it at the back of her throat for days afterward. She was one of the last to evacuate, and the paramedics later told her she’d inhaled enough toluene and acetone to warrant a night in observation. The official report ruled it an accident, but Carol could not stop replaying the sequence: if only she had noticed the motor’s odd hum earlier, if only she had insisted on a walk-through before the meeting, if only she had taken a different seat farther from the ventilation unit. The rumination became a daily ritual, a loop she could not exit.

Now, two years later, the smells still ambush her. Smoke from a neighbor’s barbecue, the burnt edge of a toast, the sharp alcohol scent of hand sanitizer in a colleague’s office—each triggers a cascade of physical reactivity: her heart pounds, her palms sweat, and she feels the same trapped, dizzy sensation she had in that stairwell. She has learned to avoid television programs that depict fires or chemical accidents, and she flips past news articles about industrial spills without reading them. Her husband, Tom, has noticed that she no longer joins him for evening walks past the old factory district, though she says only that she prefers the other route.

At work, Carol has become hypervigilant in ways that confuse her younger coworkers. She always arrives early to meetings so she can choose a seat with a clear view of the exits; she never sits with her back to a door. In any new building, she scans for emergency exits before she even unbuttons her coat. She tells herself this is just caution, but underneath there is a deeper worry: she can no longer trust her own judgment. The event proved, she feels, that she missed the signs, that she could not protect herself. This self-doubt has seeped into every decision. She second-guesses the wording of policy memos, rechecks her calculations three times, and hesitates before voicing an opinion in strategy sessions. She used to be known for her decisive analysis; now she leaves meetings wondering if she had said something wrong.

Most troubling to Carol is a numbness she cannot shake. She still feels fear and anxiety, but joy, curiosity, and even anger seem blunted, as if they belong to someone else’s life. She watches herself interact with Tom and their adult children, going through motions, but the emotional texture feels gone. She has come to believe that the chemical exposure did something permanent to her—that her normal emotional range was lost somewhere in that smoke.

What finally brought Carol to seek help was a small but telling moment: at a family dinner, her son lit a scented candle that smelled faintly of sandalwood and smoke. She gasped, dropped her fork, and fled the table. Tom found her in the bathroom, trembling, and this time she could not dismiss it as simple caution. She is afraid that the vigilance will never end, and even more afraid that she will never feel like herself again. But she also hopes—quietly, as if hoping itself might be reckless—that someone can show her how to untangle the past from the present, and maybe help her trust her own senses once more.
